{{Short description|American award for mathematics research books}}
The '''Joseph L. Doob Prize''' of the [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS) awards $5,000 (U.S.) every three years for "a single, relatively recent, outstanding research book that makes a seminal contribution to the research literature, reflects the highest standards of research exposition, and promises to have a deep and long-term impact in its area."<ref name=DoobPrize>{{cite web|title=Joseph L. Doob Prize|website=American Mathematical Society|url=http://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/ams-prizes/doob-prize}}</ref> The prize, endowed in 2005 by [[Paul Halmos|Paul]] and [[Virginia Halmos]], is named in honor of AMS President [[Joseph L. Doob]],<ref name=DoobPrize/> who was Paul Halmos's doctoral advisor in the department of mathematics at the [[University of Illinois]]. According to Paul Halmos, "Doob was the first well-informed modern mathematician in the department".<ref>{{cite book|author=Halmos, Paul|year=2020|page=51|title=I Want to Be a Mathematician|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TsH2DwAAQBAJ&q=doob+was+the+first|isbn=978-0-88385-445-7|postscript=; 1st edition 1985, Springer-Verlag }}</ref> In order for a mathematical research book to be eligible for the prize, it must have been published within the past 6 calendar years of the year of its nomination.<ref name=DoobPrize/> The prize was originally named the AMS Book Prize,<ref>{{cite web|title=William P. Thurston Receives 2005 AMS Book Prize|website=American Mathematical Society|date=January 6, 2005|url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=347}}</ref> but after the first award was renamed the Doob Prize.<ref>{{cite journal|title=2008 Doob Prize|journal=Notices of the AMS|date=April 2008|volume=55|issue=4|pages=503–504|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200804/tx080400503p.pdf}}</ref>

==Recipients==
*2005 —[[William P. Thurston]] for ''Three-dimensional Geometry and Topology'' (Princeton University Press 1997)
*2008 — [[Enrico Bombieri]] and [[Walter Gubler]] for ''Heights in Diophantine Geometry'' (Cambridge University Press 2006)
*2011 — [[Peter Kronheimer]] and [[Tomasz Mrowka]] for ''Monopoles and Three Manifolds'' (Cambridge University Press 2007)
*2014 — [[Cédric Villani]] for ''Optimal Transport: Old and New'' (Springer Verlag 2009)
*2017 — [[John Friedlander]] and [[Henryk Iwaniec]] for ''Opera de Cribro'' (AMS, 2010)
*2020 — [[René Carmona]] and {{ill|François Delarue|fr|François Delarue (mathématicien)}} for ''Probabilistic Theory of Mean Field Games with Applications'' (Springer, 2018)
*2023 — [[Bjorn Poonen]] for "Rational Points on Varieties" (American Mathematical Society, 2017)
*2026 — [[Semyon Dyatlov]] and [[Maciej Zworski]] for ''Mathematical Theory of Scattering Resonances'' (AMS 2019)<ref>{{cite web |title=Dyatlov and Zworski to Receive 2026 Joseph L. Doob Prize |url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=7556 |website=www.ams.org |date=November 10, 2025}}</ref>
